extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of moral philosophy; readers and critics of Kantian ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic critique of Kant's ethical system focusing on the form of duty, the a priori grounding of the moral law, universality, and the correct basis for moral worth. It examines what an ethical principle is (the 'what') versus its foundation (the 'why').

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperative Form of Ethics / Doctrine of Duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethics cast in an imperative form (doctrine of duties) which treats moral worth as fulfilment or violation of duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues this imperative form is historically derived from theological morals (Decalogue) and therefore implicitly assumes dependence on a commanding will that announces reward or punishment. As a criterion for evaluating an ethical system, one should check whether the use of imperative language covertly imports theological hypotheses (commands, sanctions) and whether those assumptions are justified for a non-theological ethics. Antipattern: accepting 'thou shalt'/'duty' language uncritically without grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of the Imperative — avoid hidden theological assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The imperative conception of duty presupposes 'another will' giving commands; Kant borrowed this without examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a proposed ethical imperative silently depends on theological premises. If so, either make the theological premise explicit or avoid employing imperative formulations as foundational claims in a secular/philosophical system. Example: substituting 'categorical' for 'absolute' can mask theological origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties towards ourselves (scepticism about their ethical status)
rubrics_metrics.description: Duties to oneself are either based on right (impossible by volenti non fit injuria) or on love (redundant because ethics addressing love comes too late).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat claims of duties-to-self with skepticism: check whether the supposed duty really rests on right (justice) or on prudence/hygiene/affective considerations better handled elsewhere. Example: self-preservation and suicide require deeper grounds than ordinary ethical argument; class many 'self-duties' as outside strict morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish ethics from prudence, hygiene, and worldly wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: Many items listed as duties (e.g., dietetic control of onanism, hygienic prescriptions) belong to prudence or medicine rather than Morals proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating moral prescriptions, separate genuine ethical obligations from rules of prudence, health, or social expediency. Antipattern: treating hygienic or prudential advice as moral duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of sexual vices by ethical relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Onanism is mainly a childish/medical vice; bestiality is an offence against the species (abstract), while paederastia (seduction of the young) properly falls under Justice because it wrongs another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sexual misconduct by asking whether it constitutes injustice (harms another's autonomy/experience) or is a private/medical matter. Use justice-based criteria for interpersonal sexual wrongs (e.g., exploitation of minors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Law should not be empirical — a priori formalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Kant asserts the Moral Law rests solely on conceptions of pure Reason and is knowable a priori, i.e., independent of internal or external experience; thus it must be formal (about the form of actions), not material (about their essence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an evaluative criterion, check whether an ethical principle is claimed a priori and whether that claim makes it merely formal (concerned with form/universality) rather than substantive. Consider whether purely formal a priori laws can meaningfully govern concrete human motives and conduct. Antipattern: presenting as 'a priori' a law that silently depends on empirical facts about human nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid grounding morality in contingent facts about human nature (no anthropological foundation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral principle must not be derived from special human dispositions, feelings, or tendencies; Kant rejects basing morality on empirical facts of consciousness or on anthropology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing or assessing a moral theory, ensure it does not illegitimately appeal to contingent human traits as the foundation of universal obligation. Conversely, the critic warns that excluding all empirical content risks producing an empty formalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality / Formal lawfulness as the content of Kantian moral law
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the a priori moral law cannot be material, its substance is the conception of lawfulness — what is universally valid. Kant's formulation: 'Act only in accordance with that precept which you can also wish should be a general law for all rational beings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the universalizability test to evaluate maxims: can the maxim be willed as a universal law? But also critically ask whether reducing morality to mere universal form captures morally relevant material features (consequences, motives). Example: examine whether applying universalizability ignores intentions or particular human conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not illegitimately hypostatize Reason (avoid metaphysical leaps)
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not treat Reason as a self-existent hypostatic essence or posit 'rational beings' as a genus detached from the known species 'man.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a theory illegitimately abstracts human attributes into independent metaphysical entities. Ethical claims that rest on such hypostases should be scrutinized for hidden assumptions (e.g., immortality of rational soul).

rubrics_metrics.name: Basis of moral worth: intention vs maxim (motivation matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kant places moral worth in actions done from duty as such (the maxim); the author objects and insists that the intention alone decides moral worth — identical acts can be judged differently according to intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating moral worth, investigate the actor's intention and not merely adherence to a maxim or external conformity to duty. Antipattern: praising 'loveless' dutiful action as morally superior to action motivated by sympathy or love.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and honesty in definitions (duty defined transparently)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kant's definition: 'Duty is the necessity of an action out of respect for the law.' This is criticized as convoluted and as possibly concealing theological or coercive undertones; 'Achtung' (respect) is used in place of 'Gehorsam' (obedience) to veil sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand clear, unambiguous definitions of key moral concepts. Beware euphemistic replacements (e.g., 'respect' for 'obedience') that mask underlying assumptions. Definitions should not be artificially paraphrased to hide their real meaning (e.g., 'necessity' for 'ought'/'shall').

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish principle (ὅ,τι) from basis (διότι)
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle (what is prescribed) must be kept separate from its basis (the reason or ground of obligation); many moralists conflate them, disguising the absence of a genuine foundation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate ethical systems by asking (a) what the fundamental principle prescribes (the 'what') and (b) what reasons or justifications are offered for it (the 'why'). Avoid conflating a neat principle with a purported proof of its ultimate foundation. Example: 'Do no harm; help others' as the principle distinct from any attempted metaphysical justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental ethical principle should be simple and explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: The author offers as the simplest principle: 'Neminem laede, immo omnes, quantum potes, juva' (Do harm to no one; rather help all people, as far as lies in your power).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a criterion for constructing or appraising ethical systems, prefer concise, explicit formulations of the core principle that other precepts can be seen to paraphrase. Test whether purportedly deep formulas reduce to this kind of common-sense principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical efficacy and connection to real human motives
rubrics_metrics.description: A purely formal a priori moral law may lack practical force and fail to correspond to empirical reality (the text notes Kant admits doubt whether it has ever been followed in practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a moral principle is capable of guiding real conduct and affecting human motives, not merely formal correctness. Antipattern: endorsing an abstract 'ought' that has no discernible application or motivational power in human life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency in derivations — avoid covert assumptions in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Kant's derivation of the Categorical Imperative is described as a subtle thought process that often hides premises; disciples mistakenly treat the imperative as a fact of consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a moral law is deduced, require explicit statement of premises and avoid hidden petitio principii. Check whether the derivation truly avoids empirical assumptions or secretly presumes them. Example: insist that claims 'investigated entirely a priori' actually do not smuggle in anthropological content.
